answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is genuine Twain, and the popular wording is exact. It is the epigraph that opens chapter 8 of The Tragedy of Pudd’nhead Wilson (1894) — one of the maxims Twain attributes in-book to “Pudd’nhead Wilson’s Calendar.” The sentence appears word for word in the published text at Project Gutenberg ↗.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Serialized in The Century Magazine, 1893–94; published as a novel in 1894

source.excerpt:
The holy passion of Friendship is of so sweet and steady and loyal and enduring a nature that it will last through a whole lifetime, if not asked to lend money.—Pudd’nhead Wilson’s Calendar

Consider well the proportions of things. It is better to be a young June-bug than an old bird of paradise.—Pudd’nhead Wilson’s Calendar

It is necessary now, to hunt up Roxy.
trail: Primary text. The complete novel at Project Gutenberg ↗ carries the sentence verbatim as the epigraph to Chapter VIII, “Marse Tom Tramples His Chance.”
Second transcription. Wikisource’s chapter 8 ↗ shows the same wording, signed “Pudd’nhead Wilson’s Calendar,” followed by a second calendar entry and the chapter’s opening line.
Reference index. Wikiquote’s page for the novel ↗ lists the line in its sourced quotations with the citation “Ch. 8.”
Period printing. A scan of the 1894 American Pub. Co. edition, digitized by Google from the New York Public Library, is available at the Internet Archive ↗.
source.excerptNote: The two calendar maxims stand together at the head of chapter 8 — headed plainly “Chapter VIII” in the 1894 printing, and titled “Marse Tom Tramples His Chance” in the later editions Gutenberg and Wikisource follow — immediately above the sentence that returns the story to Roxy.

author.name: Mark Twain
author.heading: About Mark Twain
author.bio: Mark Twain was the pen name of Samuel Langhorne Clemens, the Missouri-born printer, riverboat pilot and newspaperman who became the most quoted American writer of the nineteenth century. The Tragedy of Pudd’nhead Wilson — serialized in The Century Magazine in 1893–94 and published as a book in 1894 — is a courtroom novel about swapped infants, fingerprints and the absurdity of the colour line. Its chapters are headed by aphorisms from a fictional almanac, which is where this line lives.

misattribution.heading: What gets garbled
misattribution.intro: The attribution itself is sound — this really is Twain, and the popular wording is the published wording. What travels badly is everything around it: the book, the fictional frame, and, on at least one large aggregator, the author’s name.

items.why: Quotefancy runs the line under King’s name, welded without punctuation onto a second sentence about the silence of our friends — see the page itself ↗. The result is one run-on “quote” stitched from two sources, and only the first half has a documented home. The King half is widely but not verifiably attributed: researchers report that it appears in none of his published writings or speeches, and point to a 1986 Elie Wiesel line as the likelier ancestor (WIST collects the searches ↗). Nothing in King is the source of the Twain sentence either way — it was in print decades before he was born.

items.who: Twain speaking in his own voice
items.why: Quote sites print it as a free-floating Twain epigram. In the book it is an entry from a fictional almanac kept by the character David “Pudd’nhead” Wilson, set above chapter 8 and signed “Pudd’nhead Wilson’s Calendar” — as Wikisource shows ↗. Twain wrote it; a character is nominally saying it.
Twain capitalises Friendship, which is half the mock-solemnity of the sentence. Reposts routinely flatten it — the lower-case form is what that same Quotefancy page ↗ carries.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is Twain’s, exactly as quoted, and its home address is the chapter 8 epigraph of The Tragedy of Pudd’nhead Wilson (1894) — readable in full at Project Gutenberg ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Every chapter of Pudd’nhead Wilson opens with a scrap from a calendar its title character keeps for his own amusement. In the novel the townspeople read these “playful trifles in the solidest earnest,” miss the irony completely, and conclude that Wilson is a fool — which is the joke Twain is actually telling. The friendship maxim is a small machine of that kind: four adjectives of pulpit warmth (“sweet and steady and loyal and enduring”) stacked so a six-word conditional can knock them all over.

Chapter 8 is where Roxy comes back to town and goes looking for the son she swapped in the cradle, and where he refuses her. Pairing a gag about friendship surviving everything except a loan with a chapter about a family bond collapsing on contact with money is not an accident of layout.
detailsBody: The calendar epigraphs proved more portable than the novel. Twain reused the device in Following the Equator (1897) under the heading “Pudd’nhead Wilson’s New Calendar,” and a great many of the one-liners now circulating under his name are calendar entries lifted out of one book or the other — genuinely his, but written as the sayings of a character.
Chapter 8 carries a second calendar entry immediately after this one: “Consider well the proportions of things. It is better to be a young June-bug than an old bird of paradise.”
context.pull: The setup is a sermon. The punchline is a bank statement.
